a: <speak version="1.0" xmlns="http://www.w3.org/2001/10/synthesis" xml:lang="en-GB"><voice name="en-GB-RyanNeural"><prosody rate="-4%">Why Nineteen Eighty-Four Still Matters.<break time="1500ms"/>Imagine living in a world where the government watches everything you do, controls what you think and can change the truth whenever it wants. This is the dystopian world of Nineteen Eighty-Four, published by George Orwell in 1949. The book is about power, fear and freedom, and it makes the reader think about how society should work. Although some parts of the story are difficult and may feel slow, I believe people should read it, because the world it is set in is fascinating, its message is becoming more relevant because of technology, and the concepts Orwell invented, such as Newspeak and thoughtcrime, are interesting.<break time="1400ms"/>Firstly, the world in which the novel is set is fascinating. Orwell describes Airstrip One, a grey version of London where telescreens watch people in their own homes and posters of Big Brother hang on every wall. Every detail shows how complete the Party’s control is, from the Two Minutes Hate, where everyone screams at the face of the enemy, to the Ministry of Truth, where Winston rewrites old newspapers so that the Party is never wrong. Therefore, the reader is drawn into Winston’s world from the very first page.<break time="1400ms"/>Secondly, the message of the novel is becoming more relevant because of modern technology. In the book, the telescreen both watches and listens, and it can never be switched off. Today, most of us carry smartphones with cameras and microphones, and companies and governments can collect enormous amounts of information about us. Furthermore, the Party’s habit of changing the past reminds us of how easily fake news and edited images spread online. Orwell could not have imagined the internet, yet his warning fits our time remarkably well. As a result, the book feels less like science fiction and more like a description of a possible future.<break time="1400ms"/>Finally, the concepts Orwell invented, such as Newspeak and thoughtcrime, are some of the most interesting parts of the book. Newspeak is a language designed to have fewer words every year, so that rebellious thoughts become impossible because there are no words to express them. Thoughtcrime means that even thinking against the Party is a crime, which is why Winston is in danger the moment he opens his diary. It is true that the parts explaining these ideas, such as Goldstein’s book, can feel slow. However, they are what make the novel so thought-provoking, and words like “Big Brother” and “doublethink” are still used today. In short, Orwell’s ideas have outlived the story itself.<break time="1400ms"/>In conclusion, although some parts of Nineteen Eighty-Four are slow and demanding, it is well worth reading because of its fascinating world, its increasingly relevant message and the original concepts Orwell created. The novel reminds us how valuable freedom and truth are, and how easily they can be taken away. Everyone should read it, because the best way to protect our freedom is to understand how it can be lost.<break time="3000ms"/></prosody></voice></speak>
